pools.title: Who mined the {{total}} blocks of the last 24 hours?

intro: No central bank decides which transactions are valid on Ergo. That job belongs to miners — people who use their computers to secure the network, and get paid in ERG for it.

what.title: What do miners do?
what.p1: Every miner does three things, over and over:
what.s1: Take the transactions waiting in the mempool and check they're valid.
what.s2: Assemble them into a candidate block that points to the latest block in the chain.
what.s3: Change one spare number in the block (the nonce), recompute the block's fingerprint (its hash), and check whether it's small enough. Repeat billions of times.
what.p2: Step 3 is like rolling dice billions of times hoping for an extremely rare number. There's no shortcut — you just try lots of times, very fast. The combined guessing speed of the whole network is called the hashrate.
what.figAlt: A mining rig fills in the nonce of a candidate block and hashes it again and again. Nonces 1 to 3 give hashes that are too big; nonce 4 gives a hash starting with zeros that is small enough, so the block joins the chain and the miner earns the block reward.
what.figCaption: Mining is guessing: change the nonce, hash, repeat until the hash is small enough. The lucky guess wins the block reward.

reward.title: The reward
reward.p1: The miner who finds a block receives two things:
reward.block: The block reward: newly created ERG according to the emission schedule.
reward.current: At the current height, the miner receives {{reward}} ERG per block straight away.
reward.fees: Transaction fees: the total fees of every transaction in the block.
reward.p2: As the block reward shrinks, transaction fees and the re-emission mechanism (EIP-27) become more and more important for keeping miners securing the network.

difficulty.title: Self-adjusting difficulty
difficulty.p1: If more miners join, blocks get found faster. To keep the pace at roughly one block every 2 minutes, the network automatically raises the difficulty — meaning the hash has to be even smaller. When miners leave, the difficulty comes back down.
difficulty.p2: There's a simple relationship: hashrate ≈ difficulty ÷ 120 seconds. That's how the explorer estimates the whole network's hashrate without asking any miner. Details in Difficulty & nBits.

gpu.title: Why can GPUs still mine Ergo?
gpu.p1: Today Bitcoin can only be mined with expensive, specialized ASIC machines, concentrated in the hands of a few companies. Ergo took a different path: its Autolykos v2 algorithm is memory-hard — every attempt needs to read data from a large table in memory. Ordinary graphics cards (GPUs) have fast memory and do this very well, while building an ASIC that dramatically outperforms them is much harder and less worthwhile.
gpu.p2: The result: anyone with a GPU rig can help secure the network.
gpu.note: Learn how Autolykos works and what the pk, w, n and d fields in every block mean in Autolykos v2.

pool.title: Solo mining or a pool?
pool.p1: With thousands of miners, the chance of a small rig finding a block on its own is very low — you might wait months. So most miners join a pool: they combine their power and split the rewards according to their contribution. Smaller payouts, but far more regular.
pool.p2: The spread across pools is worth watching: if one pool controlled more than half the hashrate, it could in theory disrupt the network. Miners can switch pools at any time — a way of “voting with their feet” that keeps the network decentralized.

start.title: Getting started: pools and a miner
start.p1: To mine you need two things: a pool to join and mining software for your GPU. Here are three pools popular with Ergo miners, a new kind of decentralized pool, and an open-source miner.

items.2miners: One of the largest Ergo pools, with servers in Europe, the USA and Asia. Works with most popular miners, and can also pay you in Bitcoin instead of ERG.
items.herominers: A long-running multi-coin pool with servers around the world. Offers PPS+ and PROPX payouts, a solo-mining option, and per-rig statistics.
items.sigmanauts: A community pool run as a DAO by the Sigmanauts, Ergo's volunteer community group. Uses PPLNS payouts, pays weekly bonus tokens, and was the first pool to collect <rent>storage rent</rent> on boxes older than four years.
items.soat: An open-source (MIT) GPU miner with no dev fee: NVIDIA via CUDA, AMD via Vulkan, on Linux and Windows. It comes with a simple app — pick a pool, paste your address, click Mine — plus a gaming mode that slows the cards down so you can play while you mine. Needs a GPU with at least 8 GB of memory, and that requirement slowly grows over time.
items.lithos: Not a company-run pool but a decentralized pool protocol: smart contracts on Ergo check each miner's work and pay them directly, with no pool operator holding the rewards. You run your own Ergo node plus the Lithos client. It's still early — the testnet is live and mainnet is in pre-release — so it's aimed at more technical miners for now.

start.note: Fees and payout rules change over time, so check each pool's own site before you start. Only download miners from their official release page: antivirus programs often flag even genuine GPU miners, so a warning (or the lack of one) won't tell you whether a download is fake.
